extracted.intended_audience: students, reformers, and policymakers considering electoral reform; readers of political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for designing or evaluating systems of representation and voting (who may vote, weighted voting, indirect election, secret vs public ballot, and minority protection). Grounded in political-theory argumentation rather than technical electoral engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural voting justified by individual mental superiority / education
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only thing which can justify reckoning one person's opinion as equivalent to more than one is individual mental superiority, and what is wanted is some approximate means of ascertaining that."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that if plurality of votes is to be allowed, its justification must rest on mental superiority (education, intelligence). Practical tests suggested include occupation as a proxy (employer of labour, foreman, skilled trades, banker, merchant, manufacturer), successful performance of superior functions, membership/practice of the liberal professions, university graduation, or passage through higher-school courses under reliable conditions. Conditions such as a period of perseverance in an occupation (e.g., three years) are suggested to deter nominal engagement for the sake of votes. Any scheme should be open to discussion in detail, and the precise arrangements are not prescribed, but the principle is that superior influence should reflect superior mental capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to basing voting weight on property
rubrics_metrics.description: "I consider it entirely inadmissible, unless as a temporary makeshift, that the superiority of influence should be conferred in consideration of property."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property is acknowledged as an imperfect test (accident and fortune affect station), odious as a permanent foundation for electoral privilege, and likely to compromise the principle's legitimacy. Mill allows that pecuniary circumstance has been used as an imperfect proxy but urges that connecting plurality of votes to pecuniary qualification is objectionable and would render permanent maintenance impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation-based qualification as an imperfect but usable test
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the absence of [a national education/exam system], the nature of a person's occupation is some test. An employer of labour is on the average more intelligent than a labourer ... A foreman is generally more intelligent than an ordinary labourer, and a labourer in the skilled trades than in the unskilled."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill proposes using occupation (and success in performing superior functions) as an approximate test of intelligence when direct educational testing is unavailable. He stresses requiring evidence of sustained engagement (e.g., three years) to avoid nominal claims. Such occupational categories could entitle persons to two or more votes subject to safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special admission by examination or certificate to claim extra votes
rubrics_metrics.description: "There ought to be voluntary examinations at which any person whatever might present himself, might prove that he came up to the standard of knowledge and ability laid down as sufficient, and be admitted, in consequence, to the plurality of votes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill recommends voluntary, open examinations (or recognized certificates/university degrees) as routes to plural voting. Examinations should be genuinely accessible to all comers and secure that teaching is real (not a mere pretense). He cites the University of Oxford's local/middle-class associate examination as an example of a useful test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural voting must not enable class domination
rubrics_metrics.description: "The plurality of votes must on no account be carried so far that those who are privileged by it, or the class (if any) to which they mainly belong, shall outweigh by means of it all the rest of the community."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any grading or distinctions must not be arbitrary and must be understandable and acceptable to the public conscience. While recognizing some superior influence for the better educated is defensible, it must stop short of enabling that class to practice class legislation; limits and transparency are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural voting should be open to poorest individuals who can prove qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is an absolutely necessary part of the plurality scheme that it be open to the poorest individual in the community to claim its privileges, if he can prove that, in spite of all difficulties and obstacles, he is, in point of intelligence, entitled to them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill insists on voluntary avenues (exams/certificates) that do not exclude the poor; privileges should not be confined to presumptions tied to wealth. A privilege not allowed to a poor person who can demonstrate the required standard would be unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proportional representation (Hare) to secure benefits of universal suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: "I should not despair of the operation even of equal and universal suffrage, if made real by the proportional representation of all minorities, on Mr. Hare's principle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill sees proportional representation as a means of making universal suffrage practicable by securing minority representation and mitigating the evils of majority rule. He treats proportional representation as a possibly preferable route to realize benefits of broad suffrage while protecting minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural voting as preferable to equal universal suffrage under some conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: "But if the best hopes which can be formed on this subject were certainties, I should still contend for the principle of plural voting ... I do not look upon equal voting as among the things which are good in themselves ... I look upon it as only relatively good; less objectionable than inequality of privilege grounded on irrelevant or adventitious circumstances, but in principle wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that equal man-for-man voting is not intrinsically ideal because it places ignorance on equal footing with knowledge; plural voting (if properly limited and justly administered) may better express the state's valuation of mental qualifications and preserve the 'spirit' of institutions that encourage excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect (two-stage) elections generally undesirable except in special contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: "This contrivance [primary electors choosing other electors who elect members] was probably intended ... to be less moved than the Demos by the gusts of popular passion ... but ... every benefit of indirect election which is attainable at all is attainable under direct; ... the latter has considerable disadvantages peculiar to itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues indirect elections reduce political engagement, fail to cultivate public spirit and intelligence among the many, enable intrigue and corruption (small electorates are easy to bribe), and weaken representatives' accountability to constituents. He allows exceptions where electors have significant other functions or in federal contexts (e.g., U.S. Senate chosen by state legislatures), where indirect election can be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: If electors are pledged or partisan, indirect election degenerates into the same effect as direct election
rubrics_metrics.description: "The electors are always chosen under an express engagement to vote for a particular candidate ... the moment the double stage of election began to have any effect, it would begin to have a bad effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, when electors are chosen as pledged partisans, the indirect system merely replicates direct party-ticket voting and loses any theoretical advantage; the capacity for evasion of responsibility and corruption remains. Mill uses the American Electoral College as an example of this practical outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of voting (secret vs publicity): prefer publicity for public-trust spirit; secrecy exceptional
rubrics_metrics.description: "The question of greatest moment in regard to modes of voting is that of secrecy or publicity ... The spirit of vote by ballot--the interpretation likely to be put on it in the mind of an elector, is that the suffrage is given to him for himself--for his particular use and benefit, and not as a trust for the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cautions that the secret ballot can foster the impression that voting is a private right rather than a public trust, undermining accountability and the public spirit. He acknowledges secrecy is justifiable and imperative in some cases (to protect electors from evils) but considers such cases exceptions rather than the rule. Mode of voting should be chosen with attention to the institutional 'spirit' it instills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex is irrelevant to political rights; women should have suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: "I consider [difference of sex] to be as entirely irrelevant to political rights as difference in height or in the color of the hair ... the accident of sex, no more than the accident of skin, will be deemed a sufficient justification for depriving its possessor of the equal protection and just privileges of a citizen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues women's political exclusion has no principled basis; they have the same stake in good government, often greater need for protection, and participation would raise women's dignity and improve the quality of political deliberation. He rejects sex-based disqualification even where suffrage conditions are otherwise personal (property, head-of-household, tax payment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow multiple votes by registration in distinct constituencies only cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: "A person may have a double vote by other means than that of tendering two votes at the same hustings; he may have a vote in each of two different constituencies ... I would not abolish it where it exists ... until a truer test of education is adopted, it would be unwise to dispense with even so imperfect a one as is afforded by pecuniary circumstances."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill recognizes existing practices (double votes via registration in distinct constituencies) as imperfect proxies for merit and suggests not abolishing them hastily; he also notes practical complications with such privileges under schemes like proportional representation (Mr. Hare's plan) and the need to weigh trade-offs.
